stem: A 21-year-old woman has fatigue and a fixed, widely split second heart sound. Echocardiography shows a defect in the center of the atrial septum at the fossa ovalis with left-to-right shunting.
oneliner: 21F + fatigue + fixed widely split S2 + defect at fossa ovalis + left-to-right atrial shunt → which embryologic error?
ask: Which embryologic error most likely caused this defect?

options.B: Failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to spiral
options.C: Excessive resorption of the septum primum
options.D: Incomplete fusion of the membranous interventricular septum
options.E: Anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular septum

whyNot.A: Gives a **lower** atrial defect (ostium primum) at the AV valve level, not at the fossa ovalis
whyNot.B: Gives **transposition** of the great arteries, a great-vessel defect, not an atrial defect
whyNot.D: Produces a **ventricular** septal defect with a holosystolic murmur
whyNot.E: The cause of **tetralogy of Fallot**, with cyanosis and right ventricular outflow obstruction

answer: Excessive resorption of the septum primum (or deficient septum secundum)
why: A defect at the **fossa ovalis** is an **ostium secundum ASD**, the most common type. It arises from **excessive resorption of septum primum** or a **deficient septum secundum**, leaving a **left-to-right shunt** and **fixed split S2**.

idea.rule: Secundum ASD = middle of the septum = primum resorbed too much or secundum too small.
also: Primum ASD comes from endocardial cushion failure
Patent foramen ovale: septa fail to fuse after birth
Paradoxical embolism can pass through an ASD

stem: A 3-year-old girl who is not cyanotic has a loud holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border. Cardiac catheterization shows an oxygen step-up in the right ventricle.
oneliner: 3F + acyanotic + holosystolic murmur at left lower sternal border + oxygen step-up in right ventricle → which part of the septum?
ask: Which part of the septum is most likely abnormal?

whyNot.A: Muscular defects also shunt at the ventricle but are **less common** and often close; the membranous part is the **most likely** site
whyNot.B: An **atrial** defect, so the step-up would be in the **right atrium**, not the ventricle
whyNot.C: An **atrial** defect, so the step-up would be in the **right atrium**, not the ventricle
whyNot.D: Its anterior displacement causes **tetralogy of Fallot**, which would make her **cyanotic**

why: The **oxygen step-up in the right ventricle** places the shunt at the **ventricular** level. Most VSDs are **membranous**, from **incomplete fusion** of the membranous septum, giving a **holosystolic murmur**.

idea.rule: Step-up in the right ventricle = VSD, and most VSDs are membranous.
also: Step-up in the right atrium suggests ASD
Large VSD can cause Eisenmenger syndrome
Muscular VSDs often close on their own

stem: In a lineage-tracing study of a mouse embryo, researchers label one pair of pharyngeal arch arteries and trace which one later becomes the ductus arteriosus together with the proximal pulmonary arteries.
oneliner: Experiment: pharyngeal arch artery traced to ductus arteriosus and proximal pulmonary arteries → which arch?

whyNot.A: Contributes only to a small part of the **maxillary artery**
whyNot.C: Forms the **common carotid** and proximal internal carotid arteries
whyNot.D: Forms the **aortic arch** on the left and the **proximal right subclavian** artery
whyNot.E: Regresses completely and **forms no vessel** in humans

why: The **6th arch** forms the **proximal pulmonary arteries** and the **ductus arteriosus** (on the left). The **3rd** forms the common carotid and the **4th** the aortic arch and right subclavian.

idea.rule: 3rd = carotid, 4th = aortic arch and right subclavian, 6th = pulmonary arteries and ductus.
also: Ductus arteriosus later becomes the ligamentum arteriosum
Persistent 4th arch anomalies include a right aortic arch
Recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks around the 6th arch derivative on the left
